metadata.title: Immediate Sequential Bilateral Cataract Surgery (ISBCS) during COVID recovery: RCOphth/UKISCRS rapid advice document
metadata.organization: RCOphth COVID-19 Review Team and UK and Ireland Society of Cataract and Refractive Surgeons (UKISCRS)
metadata.summary: This rapid advice addresses how cataract surgery units may offer immediate sequential bilateral cataract surgery (ISBCS) during recovery from the COVID pandemic. It covers patient selection, surgical precautions, consent and postoperative arrangements, while considering the risks associated with hospital attendance. It does not specifically address bilateral surgery undertaken primarily for refractive purposes or clear lens extraction for clinical reasons.

target_population: Adults for whom cataract surgery is indicated in both eyes
Patients with unilateral cataract and high refractive error when expedited second eye surgery cannot be assured

conditions.name: Visually significant bilateral cataract
conditions.description: Cataract affects both eyes, and surgery is indicated for each eye.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Visual impairment is sufficient to warrant cataract surgery in both eyes.

subtypes.name: dense or white cataract
subtypes.distinguishing_features: These cataracts are cited as examples of increased surgical complication risk when assessing suitability for ISBCS.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess axial length and inform intraocular lens selection for each eye.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Earlier guidance suggested axial lengths of 21.5 – 26.0 mm in both eyes and an inter-eye difference of ≤ 1.5mm to reduce biometry errors. The document suggests that relaxing these limits may be appropriate if local audit data first establish biometry accuracy outside them.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When iodine allergy status is uncertain.

long_term_effects: Complications involving both eyes during or after surgery can result in long-term visual impairment.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: ISBCS outcomes should be monitored closely and compared with national standards.

conditions.name: unilateral cataract
conditions.description: In the setting of high refractive error, the document considers ISBCS for unilateral cataract if prompt second-eye surgery cannot be assured, usually only when safety is a concern or postoperative anisometropia cannot be managed another way.

therapies_index.name: ISBCS
approved_indications: Adults with visually significant cataract in both eyes when surgery is indicated for each eye and there are no absolute contraindications.

According to the NICE guidance cited in the document, consider bilateral surgery for people at low risk of ocular complications, or for those who require general anaesthesia when it poses an increased risk of complications or distress.

In the setting of high refractive error and no assurance of prompt second-eye surgery, it may be considered for unilateral cataract, usually only when safety is a concern or postoperative anisometropia cannot be managed another way.
therapies_index.administration: The second eye is operated on immediately after the first on the same surgical list. Each eye requires its own safety checks and fully separate aseptic preparation, instruments and supplies. Surgery on the second eye must be deferred if a significant complication is suspected in the first.
key_toxicities: Complications affecting both eyes may cause long-term visual impairment.
Bilateral endophthalmitis is a potentially devastating complication; its precise frequency is unknown.
Other significant complications discussed for both eyes include cystoid macular oedema, retinal detachment and toxic anterior segment syndrome.
The result of first-eye surgery cannot be used to adjust the intraocular lens choice for the second eye.
monitoring: Monitor outcomes closely and compare them with national standards.
Resolve any issue arising during first-eye surgery before deciding whether to proceed with the second eye.

therapies_index.name: cataract surgery
approved_indications: Visual rehabilitation for patients with cataract.
key_toxicities: The document identifies capsule rupture and endophthalmitis as surgical complications.
Hospital attendance for surgery entails a potential risk of contracting or transmitting COVID.

therapies_index.name: delayed second eye surgery
approved_indications: An alternative to ISBCS that patients must be free to choose after receiving information about both options.
therapies_index.administration: The second eye is operated on at a later time rather than immediately after the first.

therapies_index.name: general anaesthesia
approved_indications: Anaesthesia for cataract surgery in people who need it.
It may permit reconsideration of some relative contraindications to ISBCS when medical co-morbidity suggests that one general anaesthetic would be significantly safer than two.
key_toxicities: In some patients, general anaesthesia carries an increased risk of complications or distress.

therapies_index.name: Topical anaesthesia
therapies_index.administration: May be used with or without sedation.

therapies_index.name: sedation
approved_indications: An optional accompaniment to topical anaesthesia for ISBCS.

therapies_index.name: sub-tenons
approved_indications: An anaesthetic option for one eye during ISBCS.
therapies_index.administration: Use in one eye only; blocking both eyes is preferably avoided.

therapies_index.name: Intracameral antibiotics
approved_indications: Mandatory at the end of surgery for each eye in ISBCS, subject to an agreed local policy for known or suspected drug allergy.
therapies_index.administration: Given intracamerally at the end of surgery in both eyes. If they cannot be used under the local allergy policy, ISBCS should not proceed.

therapies_index.name: suture use
approved_indications: Wound management during ISBCS when the surgeon judges suturing necessary.
therapies_index.administration: The document advises a low threshold for its use alongside careful wound construction.

therapies_index.name: contact lens wear
approved_indications: A possible way to manage postoperative anisometropia when deciding whether ISBCS is warranted for unilateral cataract.

therapies_index.name: post-operative drops
therapies_index.administration: Patients should be able to instil the drops or have someone else available to do so.

therapies_index.name: clear shield
therapies_index.administration: At least one eye should have a clear shield; both eyes should not be patched.

toxicities.incidence: The exact frequency is unknown and is considered likely to be very low; ISBCS has not been practiced widely enough to establish an incidence under contemporary clinical practice.

management.severity: A significant complication in the first eye that increases the risk of endophthalmitis or another adverse outcome
management.actions: Defer surgery on the second eye.

prevention: Treat the operations on the two eyes as separate sterile procedures, with fresh aseptic preparation, scrubbing, gowns, gloves, preparation and draping for the second eye.
Use separate instrument trays that have undergone complete, independent sterilization cycles with indicators; prevent any contact or transfer of instruments, drugs or devices between the trays.
Consider disposable instrument sets and use different batches or lots of surgical supplies for each eye.
If feasible, use IOLs from different batches for the 2 eyes; some highly experienced ISBCS units do not require this when the manufacturer has an established safety record.
Require a thorough review by the whole surgical team before changing suppliers or surgical devices.
Administer intracameral antibiotics at the end of surgery in both eyes. For known or suspected drug allergy, follow an agreed local policy: use intracameral antibiotics or do not proceed with ISBCS.
Control and manage concomitant ocular or periocular disease before surgery.

recognition: Increased surgical time for another reason

management.actions: Resolve the issue before proceeding with surgery on the second eye.

management.severity: Suspected significant complication during first-eye surgery
management.actions: Defer surgery on the second eye, particularly when the complication raises the risk of endophthalmitis or another adverse outcome.

prevention: Consider ISBCS only on lists staffed by experienced fellow-level or consultant personnel and an experienced multidisciplinary theatre team.
Use careful wound construction and a low threshold for suturing.

toxicities.event: Incorrect intraocular lens selection or unexpected refractive outcome
prevention: Plan which eye will be operated on first and distinguish the surgical plan for each eye, including the selected IOL and astigmatism management.
At the start of each eye operation, apply the RCOphth/UKOA guidance and WHO Surgical Safety operative checklist as for a separate case; check against the original biometry documentation.

Previous guidance limited ISBCS to eyes with axial lengths of 21.5 – 26.0 mm and an inter-eye difference of ≤ 1.5mm to reduce biometry errors. If a unit relaxes these limits, local audit data should first confirm biometry accuracy outside them.

Explain that the refractive result from the first eye cannot be used to adjust the second-eye lens choice, and provide tailored counselling about refractive surprise when axial lengths fall outside the earlier limits.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Administration at the end of surgery is mandatory for both eyes. For patients with known or suspected drug allergies, an agreed local policy must specify either administration of intracameral antibiotics or not proceeding with ISBCS.
prophylaxis.duration: At the end of surgery for each eye

prophylaxis.recommendation: Separate sterile preparation, personnel scrubbing and attire, instruments, sterilization cycles, and surgical supplies are required for the two eyes; instruments, drugs and devices must not pass between the two sets.
prophylaxis.duration: Throughout preparation and surgery for both eyes

prophylaxis.recommendation: Control and manage concomitant ocular or periocular disease before surgery. Increased infection risk, including that associated with chalazion, active blepharitis, lid malposition or conjunctivitis, is listed among the absolute contraindications to ISBCS.
prophylaxis.target_population: ISBCS candidates with concomitant ocular or periocular disease

prophylaxis.recommendation: Do not patch both eyes after ISBCS; cover at least one eye with a clear shield.

infection_management.prevention: Maintain complete aseptic separation between eye operations and give intracameral antibiotics to both eyes. Defer second-eye surgery if a significant first-eye complication suggests an increased risk.
These conditions are cited as examples of increased infection risk that contraindicates ISBCS; concomitant ocular or periocular disease should be controlled and managed before surgery.
infection_management.management: Control and manage the concomitant disease before surgery.

infection_management.prevention: Discuss with the patient and family the risk associated with attending hospital for cataract surgery. Include COVID-related factors in consent and in the decision about whether and when to operate, balancing the theoretical risks of infection or transmission against prolonged visual morbidity and possible injury from poor vision.

special_populations.population: Adults with visually significant bilateral cataract
special_populations.considerations: ISBCS is considered when surgery is indicated for both eyes and no absolute contraindication is present.

special_populations.population: People at low risk of ocular complications
special_populations.considerations: NICE advises considering bilateral “simultaneous” cataract surgery for people at low risk of complications during or after surgery.
NICE advises considering bilateral “simultaneous” cataract surgery when general anaesthesia is needed and carries an increased risk of complications or distress.

special_populations.population: People with immune compromise or immunosuppression
special_populations.considerations: ISBCS requires particularly careful consideration and discussion of surgical urgency during COVID, the risk of bilateral endophthalmitis and the need to reduce hospital attendance. Before COVID, this may have been an absolute contraindication.

special_populations.population: People with co-operation difficulties or increased risk of complications
special_populations.considerations: Tremor, reduced mental capacity/dementia and dense or white cataract are relative contraindications. Some restrictions may be relaxed when GA is indicated and medical co-morbidity suggests one GA would be significantly safer than two, or when a person at higher risk of COVID needs prompt surgery without multiple admissions.

special_populations.population: People with axial lengths outside previously suggested parameters
special_populations.considerations: Earlier guidance suggested axial lengths of 21.5 – 26.0 mm in both eyes and an inter-eye difference of ≤ 1.5mm to reduce biometry errors. Relaxing these limits may be appropriate with newer equipment and formulae, but local audit data should first support biometry accuracy outside them. Consent should additionally address possible complications, refractive surprise, stereopsis and neuroadaptation.
Previous refractive surgery is an absolute contraindication to ISBCS, particularly when the patient continues to prefer spectacle independence.

special_populations.population: People with unilateral cataract and high refractive error
special_populations.considerations: ISBCS may be considered if timely second-eye surgery cannot be assured, usually only when safety concerns exist or postoperative anisometropia cannot otherwise be managed, such as with contact lens wear.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults for whom cataract surgery is indicated in both eyes, with no absolute contraindication to ISBCS. NICE also identifies people at low risk of ocular complications during and after surgery as candidates for consideration.
decision_rules: Consider ISBCS only when the patient chooses it after an informed discussion and the unit has the capacity and experience to provide it safely.

Do not select ISBCS when either eye requires concomitant surgery for glaucoma, corneal or retinal disease; when there has been significant previous eye surgery or injury, lens luxation or phacodonesis; or when the risk of postoperative corneal failure is increased, as with Fuchs’ dystrophy.

Other absolute contraindications include increased infection risk, such as chalazion, active blepharitis, lid malposition or conjunctivitis; ocular co-morbidity such as recurrent uveitis, pseudoexfoliation, or active or significant diabetic retinopathy; previous refractive surgery, particularly if spectacle independence remains important; uncontrolled concomitant glaucoma in either eye; and iodine allergy. The guidance notes that uncertain iodine allergy could be investigated with patch testing.
Control and manage concomitant ocular or periocular disease before surgery, and decide in advance which eye will be operated on first.

Treat each eye as a separate operation. Before operating on each eye, repeat the WHO Surgical Safety operative checklist in accordance with RCOphth/UKOA guidance, distinguish the surgical plans for the two eyes and check them against the original biometry documentation.

Resolve any problem arising during first-eye surgery before proceeding. Defer second-eye surgery if a significant first-eye complication is suspected, including capsule rupture, vitreous loss, zonular dialysis or an otherwise prolonged operation, particularly when the problem raises the risk of endophthalmitis or another adverse outcome.

recommended_regimens.name: ISBCS
recommended_regimens.summary: When appropriate, operate on the second eye immediately after the first eye on the same surgical list, with complete aseptic separation between the procedures. ISBCS should be considered only on lists staffed by experienced fellow-level or consultant personnel and an experienced multidisciplinary theatre team; the surgeon and hospital should have good risk-adjusted records for PCR and endophthalmitis. Topical anaesthesia, with or without sedation, is preferred; sub-tenons anaesthesia in one eye only is another stated approach.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Both eye operations take place on the same surgical list.

alternative_regimens.name: delayed second eye surgery
alternative_regimens.summary: Operate on the second eye later rather than during the first-eye surgical session.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The patient chooses this option, ISBCS is unsuitable, or a significant problem with first-eye surgery requires deferral.

not_recommended.name: ISBCS
not_recommended.reason: Do not proceed when an absolute contraindication applies or when a significant complication is suspected during first-eye surgery.

not_recommended.name: one-stop models with pre-op assessment and surgery on the same day which involve consenting on the day of surgery
not_recommended.reason: The guidance considers this consent arrangement unsuitable for ISBCS.

response_assessment.timepoint: After first-eye surgery and before second-eye surgery
response_assessment.method: Assess and resolve operative problems, including suspected capsule rupture, vitreous loss, zonular dialysis or an unexpectedly prolonged procedure.
response_assessment.interpretation: A suspected significant complication, especially one increasing the risk of endophthalmitis or another adverse outcome, requires deferral of the second operation.

response_assessment.method: Monitor outcomes closely and compare them with national standards.

supportive_care: Before the second operation, the surgeon and nurse must follow sterile routines appropriate to a wholly separate procedure; the theatre team must scrub again, put on fresh gowns and gloves, and repeat preparation and draping.

Use separate instrument trays that have undergone complete, independent sterilization cycles with indicators. Instruments, drugs and devices for the two eyes must not touch or cross between trays before or during either operation; consider disposable instrument sets.

Use different batches / lots of surgical supplies for each eye and specify this when ordering. If possible, use different IOL batches for the 2 eyes; the guidance notes that some very experienced ISBCS units do not require this when the manufacturer has a proven record.
Review any proposed change of surgical supplier or device with the entire surgical team before implementation.
Pay careful attention to wound construction and maintain a low threshold for suturing.
Give intracameral antibiotics at the end of surgery in both eyes. Establish a local policy for known or suspected drug allergy: either give intracameral antibiotics or do not undertake ISBCS.

Do not patch both eyes after surgery; at least one eye should have a clear shield. Confirm that the patient can administer postoperative drops or that another person can do so. Going home with a companion is often helpful.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Consent must leave the patient free to choose between ISBCS and delayed second-eye surgery. Explain possible immediate improvement in both eyes, the inability to adjust second-eye IOL selection in response to the first-eye result, the potential for complications in both eyes to cause lasting visual impairment, and likely postoperative support needs. Discuss bilateral endophthalmitis and other important bilateral complications, including cystoid macular oedema, retinal detachment and toxic anterior segment syndrome. The precise frequency of bilateral endophthalmitis is unknown, although estimated to be very low; the guidance says contemporary practice does not support quoting an incidence figure. Discussion and consent should be led by a surgeon; non-medically led consenters need training, documented competencies and discussion with the surgical team about ISBCS-specific risks. For all cataract surgery, discuss with the patient and family the COVID risk associated with hospital attendance and weigh, in partnership with the patient, theoretical COVID acquisition or transmission risks against prolonged visual morbidity and potential injury. Training units should protect training opportunities, consider trainee experience and performance carefully, and provide close supervision.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People needing general anaesthesia for cataract surgery when general anaesthesia itself carries an increased risk of complications or distress.
decision_rules: Consider surgery on both eyes during a single anaesthetic when the patient is otherwise suitable for ISBCS.

For some patients with dementia or tremor, cooperation-related concerns may be reconsidered if general anaesthesia is indicated and medical co-morbidity suggests one GA would be significantly safer than two.

recommended_regimens.name: ISBCS
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider consecutive operations on both eyes in one session for an eligible patient whose need for general anaesthesia makes separate procedures less suitable. Apply the separate-eye safety and aseptic requirements for ISBCS.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Both eye operations take place on the same surgical list.

alternative_regimens.name: delayed second eye surgery
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Use when chosen by the informed patient or when ISBCS is unsuitable or must be deferred.

response_assessment.timepoint: After first-eye surgery and before second-eye surgery
response_assessment.method: Assess whether first-eye surgery has produced a suspected significant complication.
response_assessment.interpretation: Defer the second operation if such a complication is suspected.

supportive_care: Maintain complete aseptic separation of the eye operations and administer intracameral antibiotics at the end of each operation.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Discuss the individual's anaesthetic risks and distress, as well as the risks and benefits of ISBCS compared with waiting for second-eye surgery.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients whose axial length in either eye falls outside the previously suggested range of 21.5 – 26.0 mm, or whose inter-eye axial-length difference exceeds the previously suggested limit of ≤ 1.5mm.
decision_rules: Previous guidance suggested restricting ISBCS to axial lengths of 21.5 – 26.0 mm in both eyes and an inter-eye difference of ≤ 1.5mm to reduce biometry errors.

The guidance suggests that these limits may be relaxed with more modern biometry equipment and formulae, but recommends first confirming biometry accuracy outside those parameters using local audit data.
Provide consent tailored to the additional risk and potential benefit associated with outlying axial lengths.

recommended_regimens.name: ISBCS
recommended_regimens.summary: ISBCS may be considered outside the previously suggested axial-length parameters if local audit data first confirm biometry accuracy; otherwise, these measurements remain a relative contraindication.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Both eye operations take place on the same surgical list.

alternative_regimens.name: delayed second eye surgery
alternative_regimens.summary: Separate the two operations, retaining the opportunity to account for the first-eye refractive result before second-eye surgery.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider when the patient prefers it or the accuracy of biometry outside the previously suggested parameters has not been confirmed by local audit.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Tailored consent should cover additional complications and refractive surprise as risks, and stereopsis and neuroadaptation as potential benefits. ISBCS forfeits the opportunity to adjust the second-eye refractive plan using the first-eye outcome.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with immune compromise or immunosuppression.
decision_rules: Treat immune compromise or immunosuppression as a relative contraindication requiring extremely careful consideration and discussion with the patient.
Consider the urgency of surgery during COVID, the risk of bilateral endophthalmitis and the need to minimise hospital attendance before deciding whether to offer ISBCS.

alternative_regimens.name: ISBCS
alternative_regimens.summary: A possible option only after particularly careful individual consideration and discussion of its risks and the need for surgery.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The patient has immune compromise or immunosuppression, and the balance of surgical urgency during COVID, bilateral endophthalmitis risk and reduced attendance supports proceeding.

alternative_regimens.name: delayed second eye surgery
alternative_regimens.summary: Perform the second operation at a later visit.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The individual risk assessment or the patient's informed choice does not support ISBCS.

supportive_care: If ISBCS is undertaken, maintain complete aseptic separation between the eyes and give intracameral antibiotics at the end of surgery in both eyes.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guidance notes that this condition might have been an absolute contraindication before COVID.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with cooperation difficulties or increased complication risk, including tremor, reduced mental capacity/dementia, or dense or white cataract.
decision_rules: Regard cooperation difficulties and increased complication risk as relative contraindications to ISBCS.
Some of these restrictions may be relaxed when GA is indicated, such as for dementia or tremor, and medical co-morbidity suggests one GA would be significantly safer than two.
The guidance also allows consideration of avoiding multiple admissions for patients at higher COVID risk when prompt surgery is required.

alternative_regimens.name: ISBCS
alternative_regimens.summary: An individually considered option despite the relative contraindication when the stated anaesthetic or admission-related circumstances support it.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: GA is indicated and medical co-morbidity suggests one GA would be significantly safer than two, or prompt surgery is needed for a patient at higher COVID risk for whom multiple admissions should be avoided.

alternative_regimens.name: delayed second eye surgery
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The cooperation or complication concerns are not outweighed by the circumstances identified for considering ISBCS, or the patient chooses delayed surgery.

response_assessment.timepoint: After first-eye surgery and before second-eye surgery
response_assessment.method: Check for suspected significant complications or an otherwise prolonged first-eye operation.
response_assessment.interpretation: Defer second-eye surgery if a significant complication is suspected.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Selection remains dependent on the patient's circumstances and informed choice.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with high refractive error for whom expedited second-eye surgery cannot be assured.
decision_rules: Consider ISBCS in this setting only usually when there is a safety concern or postoperative anisometropia cannot otherwise be managed, for example by wearing a contact lens.

alternative_regimens.name: ISBCS
alternative_regimens.summary: May be considered despite unilateral cataract in the narrowly defined high-refractive-error circumstances described by the guidance.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Expedited second-eye surgery cannot be assured and, usually, safety concerns exist or postoperative anisometropia has no other manageable solution.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guidance does not specifically cover bilateral surgery undertaken primarily for refractive purposes or clear lens extraction for clinical reasons.

artifacts.title: NICE criteria and counselling points for bilateral simultaneous cataract surgery
artifacts.source_heading: Immediate Sequential Bilateral Cataract Surgery (ISBCS) during COVID recovery: RCOphth/UKISCRS rapid advice document

rows: People at low risk of ocular complications during and after surgery.
People requiring general anaesthesia for cataract surgery when that anaesthesia presents an increased risk of complications or distress.
The possibility of immediate improvement in vision in both eyes.
The inability to select a different intraocular lens in response to the outcome of surgery on the first eye.
The possibility of lasting visual impairment if complications affect both eyes during or after surgery.
The probable need for additional help following surgery.

artifacts.description: The document attributes these criteria and discussion points to the NICE guidance on adult cataract surgery 2017 (1).
artifacts.summary: This checklist brings together the patient groups for whom NICE advises considering bilateral simultaneous cataract surgery and the benefits and risks NICE says should be discussed. It supports preoperative consideration and counselling.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It helps clinicians identify potentially suitable patients while ensuring that consent addresses consequences specific to operating on both eyes.

artifacts.title: Case selection: indications

rows: An adult has visually significant cataract in both eyes, and surgery is indicated for each eye under NICE and RCOphth / UKISCRS guidelines.

artifacts.description: Both listed indications must be met.
artifacts.summary: This checklist sets out the two requirements for selecting an adult for ISBCS. It links the need for surgery in both eyes to the absence of absolute contraindications.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It establishes the initial eligibility threshold before the unit and surgeon assess specific risks.

artifacts.title: Case selection: absolute contraindications

rows: Concurrent surgery for glaucoma or for corneal or retinal disease.
A history of significant ocular surgery or injury, lens luxation, or phacodonesis.
Elevated risk of corneal failure after surgery, such as with Fuchs’ dystrophy.
Elevated infection risk, including chalazion, active blepharitis, lid malposition, or conjunctivitis.
Ocular co-morbidity, including recurrent uveitis, pseudoexfoliation, or active or significant diabetic retinopathy.
Prior refractive surgery, particularly when the patient continues to prefer independence from spectacles.
Glaucoma that is uncontrolled in either eye.
Iodine allergy; uncertainty may be investigated by patch testing.

artifacts.description: The document states that absolute contraindications differ between units and surgeons and lists these examples.
artifacts.summary: This checklist gathers the ocular, infectious, surgical-history and allergy factors identified as absolute contraindications to ISBCS. It is intended to guide exclusion during case selection.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Recognising these factors prevents selection of patients whom the document identifies as unsuitable for immediate surgery on both eyes.

artifacts.title: Relative contraindications

rows: Earlier guidance limited ISBCS to axial lengths of 21.5 – 26.0 mm in both eyes, with an inter-eye difference of ≤ 1.5mm, to reduce biometry errors. Modern equipment and formulae may justify relaxing this restriction, but local audit should first verify accuracy outside those limits.

Immune compromise or immunosuppression requires exceptionally careful assessment and discussion. During COVID, considerations include surgical urgency, bilateral endophthalmitis risk and the need to reduce attendance; before COVID it might have been an absolute contraindication.

Difficulty cooperating or increased complication risk, such as tremor, reduced mental capacity/dementia, or dense or white cataract. Some restrictions may be relaxed when GA is indicated and medical co-morbidity suggests one GA would be significantly safer than two, or when a patient at higher risk of COVID needs prompt surgery without multiple admissions.

artifacts.description: Each factor requires consideration in the circumstances described rather than automatic exclusion.
artifacts.summary: This checklist describes qualifications concerning biometry, immune status and cooperation or procedural difficulty. It also records the circumstances in which some restrictions may be relaxed.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It supports individualised selection without treating relative contraindications as either universally prohibitive or irrelevant.

artifacts.title: Surgical considerations and separation of eye procedures

rows: Bring concurrent ocular or periocular disease under control and manage it before operating.
Decide clearly which eye will be operated on first.

At the start of surgery on each eye, follow existing RCOphth/UKOA guidance (5), including the WHO Surgical Safety operative checklist, as though each eye were a separate case. Distinguish each eye’s plan, including its selected IOL and astigmatism management, and consult the original biometry records during safety checks to reduce wrong-lens and right–left errors.

With high refractive error, ISBCS may be considered for a unilateral cataract if prompt second-eye surgery cannot be assured, usually only when safety is at issue or postoperative anisometropia cannot otherwise be managed, for example with contact lens wear.
Prefer topical anaesthesia, with or without sedation, or sub-tenons in only one eye; avoiding a block in both eyes is preferable.
Maintain complete aseptic separation between the two eye operations to minimise bilateral postoperative endophthalmitis.
Before operating on the second eye, the surgeon and nurse must follow meticulous sterile procedures and prepare it independently as a separate operation.
The theatre team must scrub again, change gowns and gloves, and repeat preparation and draping of the operative site.
Use separate instrument trays that have each completed an independent, indicator-verified sterilisation cycle.
At no point before or during either operation may instruments, drugs or devices contact or transfer between the two trays.
Use different batches / lots of surgical supplies for the two eyes and specify this when ordering.
If feasible, use IOLs from different batches for the 2 eyes; some highly experienced ISBCS units do not require this when the manufacturer is reputable and has an established track record.
Do not change surgical suppliers or devices until the full surgical team has thoroughly assessed the safety of the proposed change.
Pay careful attention to wound construction and maintain a low threshold for suturing.
Give intracameral antibiotics at the end of surgery in both eyes. Apply an agreed local policy for known or suspected drug allergies: either give intracameral antibiotics or do not undertake ISBCS.

Resolve any difficulty during first-eye surgery before proceeding. Defer second-eye surgery if a significant first-eye complication is suspected, including capsule rupture, vitreous loss, zonular dialysis or prolonged operating time for another reason, especially when the risk of endophthalmitis or another adverse outcome increases.

In training units, preserve training opportunities, assess trainee experience and performance particularly carefully, and supervise trainees closely. Initially, a senior surgeon is expected to operate on the first eye; if that surgery is uneventful, a less experienced surgeon may appropriately operate on the second. This approach may change as units gain experience training on ISCBCS cases.

artifacts.description: The checklist covers preparation, eye-specific verification, anaesthesia, mandatory aseptic separation, antibiotics, the decision to defer the second eye, and trainee supervision.
artifacts.summary: These surgical safeguards treat the two operations as distinct procedures while specifying when second-eye surgery must not proceed. They address preventable errors, infection risk and intraoperative complications.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: The checks are central to reducing bilateral harm and to deciding safely whether the planned second-eye operation can go ahead.

artifacts.title: Counselling and consenting

rows: Allow the patient an informed choice between ISBCS and postponing second-eye surgery; an ISBCS-specific information sheet and consent form may help.

Explain the potentially severe consequences of bilateral endophthalmitis and other major complications. Its exact frequency is unknown and thought likely to be very low, but current ISBCS practice is not widespread enough to support an incidence estimate for contemporary care (6).
Explain specifically that ISBCS removes the opportunity to adjust the second eye’s refractive plan in light of the first eye’s result.
Explain the likelihood and possible consequences of other serious bilateral complications, including cystoid macular oedema, retinal detachment and toxic anterior segment syndrome.
For axial lengths outside the usual range, tailor consent to the risks of additional complications and refractive surprise and the potential benefits of stereopsis and neuroadaptation.

A surgeon must lead discussion and consent for ISBCS. Where non-medical staff obtain consent, they need training and documented competence for ISBCS consent, as well as discussion with the surgical team about its particular risks.
Do not use ISBCS in a one-stop pathway that combines preoperative assessment and surgery on the same day with consent obtained on the day of surgery.

artifacts.description: The checklist separates patient choice, bilateral risks, refractive implications, responsibilities for consent and an unsuitable same-day consent model.
artifacts.summary: These points structure consent specific to ISBCS, including uncertainty about the incidence of bilateral endophthalmitis. They also identify who should lead consent and a care model in which ISBCS is unsuitable.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: They help patients make an informed choice between immediate and delayed second-eye surgery without obscuring the distinctive risks of bilateral treatment.

artifacts.title: Other considerations

rows: A companion for the journey home is often helpful.
Do not patch both eyes after ISBCS; leave at least one eye with a transparent shield.
Ensure the patient can administer postoperative drops or that someone else is arranged to do so.
Monitor outcomes closely and compare them with national standards.

artifacts.description: These points address immediate postoperative support, preservation of usable vision, drop administration and outcome surveillance.

document_sections.heading: Immediate Sequential Bilateral Cataract Surgery (ISBCS) during COVID recovery: RCOphth/UKISCRS rapid advice document
document_sections.content: The RCOphth COVID-19 Review Team and UKISCRS developed this advice in response to the pandemic; it may change. COVID has substantially constrained surgical capacity. Services need to resume cataract operations for visual rehabilitation while limiting COVID transmission. Some units are considering immediate sequential bilateral cataract surgery (ISBCS) to reduce the risks of repeated visits and make service delivery more efficient. In this approach, surgery on the second eye follows surgery on the first eye immediately on the same operating list; NICE calls it “bilateral simultaneous” surgery. NICE guidance from 2017 advises providing information about this option at the preoperative appointment when appropriate. NICE says to consider it for people at low risk of complications both during and after eye surgery, or for people requiring general anaesthesia when that anaesthesia poses increased risk or distress. NICE also advises discussing the possibility of immediate improvement in both eyes, the inability to adjust the second eye’s intraocular lens choice according to the first eye’s result, the possibility of lasting visual impairment from complications affecting both eyes, and the probable need for extra postoperative help. GMC consent guidance from 2009 requires discussion of every suitable treatment option. The 2015 Montgomery vs Lanarkshire Health Board judgment placed greater emphasis on each patient’s circumstances: doctors must take reasonable steps to explain risks material to that patient and describe alternative treatments, including conservative management. Where ISBCS is available, suitable patients should hear about its potential advantages and harms and receive enough information to choose between it and waiting for second-eye surgery. A clinician may share a personal view, but the patient’s choice takes precedence. This brief advice builds on earlier publications and is intended to help units establish local guidance for offering ISBCS safely if they want to do so and have the logistical capacity. Surgery undertaken mainly for refractive purposes and clinically indicated clear lens extraction are not specifically addressed. The proposed selection criteria may evolve with growing experience and evidence, taking account of surgeon and unit experience and patient needs. ISBCS should be considered only on lists staffed by experienced fellow-level or consultant clinicians and an experienced multidisciplinary theatre team. The surgeon and hospital should have good records for risk-adjusted surgical complications (PCR) and infection (endophthalmitis).

document_sections.heading: 1. Case selection: indications (both of the following):
document_sections.content: Both criteria are required: the adult must have visually significant cataract in both eyes, with surgery indicated for each eye under NICE and RCOphth / UKISCRS guidance; and there must be no absolute contraindication.

document_sections.heading: 2. Case selection: Absolute contra-indications vary by unit and surgeon but include:
document_sections.content: Absolute contraindications include a need for simultaneous surgery for glaucoma or corneal or retinal disease; a history of significant ocular surgery or injury, lens luxation, or phacodonesis; increased likelihood of postoperative corneal failure, such as with Fuchs’ dystrophy; and increased infection risk, such as chalazion, active blepharitis, lid malposition, or conjunctivitis. They also include ocular comorbidity such as recurrent uveitis, pseudoexfoliation, or active or significant diabetic retinopathy; previous refractive surgery, particularly when the patient still wants independence from spectacles; glaucoma that is uncontrolled in either eye; and iodine allergy. Patch testing may help resolve uncertainty about iodine allergy. Which contraindications are considered absolute varies among units and surgeons.

document_sections.heading: 3. Relative contraindications:
document_sections.content: Earlier guidance proposed limiting ISBCS to patients whose axial length in each eye is within 21.5 – 26.0 mm and whose inter-eye difference is ≤ 1.5mm, to reduce biometry errors. Newer biometry devices and formulae may justify relaxing these limits, but local audit data should first establish measurement accuracy for eyes outside them. Immune compromise or immunosuppression may have constituted an absolute contraindication before COVID; it now calls for exceptionally careful consideration and patient discussion of surgical urgency during COVID, bilateral endophthalmitis risk, and the value of fewer attendances. Difficulty cooperating and greater complication risk—for example, tremor, reduced mental capacity or dementia, or a dense or white cataract—are relative contraindications. Some may be relaxed when general anaesthesia (GA) is indicated, such as for dementia or tremor, and medical comorbidity suggests one GA would be significantly safer than two. Relaxation may also be considered to avoid repeated admissions for patients at higher COVID risk who require prompt surgery.

document_sections.heading: 4. Surgical considerations:
document_sections.content: Ocular or periocular disease occurring alongside the cataract should be controlled and treated before surgery, and the team should decide clearly which eye will be operated on first. To prevent incorrect intraocular lens implantation and other never events, especially confusion between right and left eyes, the team should follow existing RCOphth/UKOA guidance. This includes applying the WHO Surgical Safety operative checklist at the start of surgery on each eye as though it were a separate case. Plans for the two eyes must be unmistakably distinct, including the selected IOL and astigmatism management; safety checks should refer to the original biometry records. For a patient with a unilateral cataract and high refractive error, ISBCS may be considered if prompt second-eye surgery cannot be guaranteed, but ordinarily only when safety is at issue or postoperative anisometropia cannot be managed otherwise, for example with contact lenses. Topical anaesthesia is preferred, whether or not sedation is used; sub-tenons may be used in one eye only. Blocking both eyes is preferably avoided. Complete aseptic separation between the two eye operations is mandatory to minimise postoperative bilateral endophthalmitis. Before operating on the second eye, the surgeon and nurse must repeat meticulous sterile preparation and treat it as an entirely separate procedure. The theatre team should scrub again, change gown and gloves, and repeat preparation and draping of the operative site. Each eye needs a separate instrument tray processed through its own complete sterilisation cycle with indicators. Instruments, medicines, and devices assigned to one eye must never touch or cross over to those assigned to the other eye, before or during either operation. Disposable instrument sets should be considered. Supplies for the eyes should come from different batches or lots, specified when ordering. Different IOL batches should be used for the 2 eyes if possible, although some highly experienced ISBCS units do not require this when the manufacturer is reputable and has an established record. Any proposed change of supplier or surgical device needs thorough review by the entire surgical team before implementation. Wounds require careful construction and a low threshold for suturing. Intracameral antibiotics at the end of each eye’s operation are mandatory. A locally agreed approach is needed for known or suspected drug allergy: either administer intracameral antibiotics or do not undertake ISBCS. Problems encountered during first-eye surgery must be resolved before proceeding. If a significant first-eye complication is suspected—including capsule rupture, vitreous loss, zonular dialysis, or a longer operation for another reason—second-eye surgery must be postponed, particularly when endophthalmitis or another adverse outcome becomes more likely. In training units, ISBCS must not diminish training opportunities. Trainees performing these cases need especially careful assessment of experience and performance and close supervision. Initially, a senior surgeon is expected to operate on the first eye; if that operation is uneventful, a less experienced surgeon may appropriately operate on the second. This arrangement may evolve as units gain experience training on ISCBCS cases.

document_sections.heading: 5. Counselling and consenting
document_sections.content: Patients must be able to choose freely and knowledgeably between ISBCS and postponing surgery on the second eye. A dedicated ISBCS information sheet and consent form may help. Counselling should explain the possible effects of bilateral endophthalmitis, which can be particularly devastating, and of other serious complications. Its exact frequency is unknown and has been estimated to be likely very low, but ISBCS has not been practised widely enough to provide an incidence figure for contemporary care. Patients should be told explicitly that ISBCS removes the opportunity to adjust the second eye’s refractive plan using the first eye’s outcome. They should also be advised about the likelihood and potential effects of other serious bilateral complications, including cystoid macular oedema, retinal detachment, and toxic anterior segment syndrome. Axial lengths outside the proposed range call for additional individualised consent covering risks, including further complications and refractive surprise, and benefits, including stereopsis and neuroadaptation. Discussion and consent for ISBCS must be surgeon-led. Where units use consenters who are not medically qualified, those staff need training and documented competence in ISBCS consent, together with discussion with the surgical team about its particular risks. ISBCS is unsuitable for one-stop pathways that combine preoperative assessment and surgery with consent obtained on the day of surgery.

document_sections.heading: 6. Other considerations:
document_sections.content: Having a companion accompany the patient home is often helpful. Both eyes must not be patched after ISBCS; at least one should have a transparent shield. Patients must be able to administer postoperative drops or have someone arranged to do so. Outcomes should receive close surveillance and comparison with national standards. For every cataract operation at this time, clinicians should follow joint UKISCRS/RCOphth guidance and discuss with the patient and family the COVID risk associated with a hospital visit. COVID-related circumstances should inform consent and decisions about whether and when to operate. Clinicians and patients should jointly weigh the theoretical risk of acquiring or transmitting COVID against the real risks of prolonged visual morbidity and possible injury from poor sight, particularly where both eyes could be affected. COVID-19 guidance may change; the RCOphth COVID-19 web page provides updates.

recommendations.statement: Select adults for ISBCS only when visually significant bilateral cataract makes surgery indicated in both eyes under NICE and RCOphth / UKISCRS guidelines and no absolute contraindication is present.
recommendations.context: Case selection: both indications must be met.

recommendations.statement: Do not select patients for ISBCS when concomitant surgery is required for glaucoma, corneal disease or retinal disease.
recommendations.context: Absolute contraindication; these may vary by unit and surgeon.

recommendations.statement: Treat previous significant eye surgery, significant eye injury, lens luxation or phacodonesis as an absolute contraindication to ISBCS.
recommendations.context: Absolute contraindications may vary by unit and surgeon.

recommendations.statement: Treat an increased risk of postoperative corneal failure, such as with Fuchs’ dystrophy, as an absolute contraindication to ISBCS.
recommendations.context: Absolute contraindications may vary by unit and surgeon.

recommendations.statement: Treat increased infection risk, including that associated with chalazion, active blepharitis, lid malposition or conjunctivitis, as an absolute contraindication to ISBCS.
recommendations.context: Absolute contraindications may vary by unit and surgeon.

recommendations.statement: Treat ocular co-morbidity, including recurrent uveitis, pseudoexfoliation, or active or significant diabetic retinopathy, as an absolute contraindication to ISBCS.
recommendations.context: Absolute contraindications may vary by unit and surgeon.

recommendations.statement: Treat previous refractive surgery as an absolute contraindication to ISBCS, particularly when the patient continues to prefer spectacle independence.
recommendations.context: Absolute contraindications may vary by unit and surgeon.

recommendations.statement: Treat concomitant glaucoma that is uncontrolled in either eye as an absolute contraindication to ISBCS.
recommendations.context: Absolute contraindications may vary by unit and surgeon.

recommendations.statement: Treat iodine allergy as an absolute contraindication to ISBCS; patch testing could resolve uncertainty about the allergy.
recommendations.context: Absolute contraindications may vary by unit and surgeon.

recommendations.statement: Consider axial lengths outside 21.5 – 26.0 mm in both eyes, or an inter-eye difference exceeding ≤ 1.5mm, as relative contraindications under previous guidance. Relaxing those limits may be appropriate with more modern biometry equipment and formulae, but local audit data should first confirm biometry accuracy in eyes outside the stated parameters.
recommendations.rationale: The earlier limits were intended to reduce biometry errors.

recommendations.statement: Consider ISBCS extremely carefully for patients with immune compromise or immunosuppression and discuss it with them, taking into account the urgency of surgery during COVID, bilateral endophthalmitis risk and the need to minimise attendance.
recommendations.context: Relative contraindication; before COVID, this might have been an absolute contraindication.

recommendations.statement: Treat difficulties with co-operation or increased complication risk, such as tremor, reduced mental capacity/dementia, or dense or white cataract, as relative contraindications. Some restrictions may be relaxed when general anaesthesia (GA) is indicated and medical co-morbidity suggests one GA would be significantly safer than two, or when avoiding multiple admissions is important for a patient at higher COVID risk who needs expedient surgery.
Control and manage concomitant ocular or periocular disease before surgery.
Establish a clear plan for which eye will undergo surgery first.

Apply existing RCOphth/UKOA guidance, including the WHO Surgical Safety operative checklist, at the start of surgery on each eye as though each were a separate case. Distinguish each eye’s surgical plan clearly, including selected IOL and astigmatism management, and consult the original biometry documentation during all safety checks.
recommendations.rationale: These checks are intended to prevent incorrect intraocular lens implantation and other never events, particularly right–left eye errors.

recommendations.statement: In the setting of high refractive error, ISBCS may be considered for unilateral cataract when prompt second-eye surgery cannot be assured, but usually only if safety concerns exist or postoperative anisometropia cannot be managed by another means, such as contact lens wear.
Prefer topical anaesthesia, with or without sedation, or sub-tenons in one eye only; preferably avoid blocking both eyes.
Maintain complete aseptic separation between first-eye and second-eye surgery.
recommendations.rationale: The separation is intended to minimise postoperative bilateral endophthalmitis.

recommendations.statement: Before operating on the second eye, the surgeon and nurse must repeat scrupulous sterile routines and prepare it aseptically as an entirely separate procedure.
recommendations.rationale: This forms part of the required separation between the two operations.

recommendations.statement: Have the theatre team scrub, gown and glove again, and repeat preparation and draping of the surgical site for the second eye.
recommendations.rationale: This forms part of the required separation between the two operations.

recommendations.statement: Use separate instrument trays for the two eyes, each subjected to a complete, separate sterilisation cycle with indicators.
recommendations.rationale: This forms part of the required separation between the two operations.

recommendations.statement: Prevent any physical contact or crossover of instruments, drugs or devices between the two eyes’ trays before or during either operation.
recommendations.rationale: This forms part of the required separation between the two operations.

recommendations.statement: Consider disposable surgical instrument sets.
Use different batches / lots of surgical supplies for each eye and specify this when ordering them.
Use different IOL batches for the 2 eyes if possible; some highly experienced ISBCS units do not require this when the IOL manufacturer is reputable and has an established track record.
Do not change surgical suppliers or devices without a thorough review of the proposed change by the entire surgical team.
recommendations.rationale: The review is intended to establish that the proposed changes are safe.

recommendations.statement: Pay careful attention to wound architecture and maintain a low threshold for placing a suture.
Give intracameral antibiotics to both eyes at the end of surgery. Establish a local policy for known or suspected drug allergies: either give intracameral antibiotics or do not proceed with ISBCS.

Resolve any problem arising during first-eye surgery before proceeding. Defer second-eye surgery if a significant first-eye complication is suspected, including capsule rupture, vitreous loss, zonular dialysis or increased operating time for another reason, particularly when it raises the risk of endophthalmitis or another adverse outcome.

In training units, preserve access to training opportunities when introducing ISBCS. Consider trainees’ experience and performance particularly carefully and supervise their ISBCS cases closely; initially, a senior surgeon is expected to operate on the first eye, after which a less experienced surgeon may appropriately operate on the second eye if the first operation was uneventful.
recommendations.context: The approach to training may change as units gain experience with ISBCS cases.

recommendations.statement: Allow patients to choose freely and on an informed basis between ISBCS and delayed second-eye surgery; a patient information sheet and consent form specific to ISBCS may help.
Ensure patients understand the potential consequences of bilateral endophthalmitis and other significant complications.
recommendations.rationale: Bilateral endophthalmitis can be particularly devastating. Its precise frequency is unknown, and ISBCS has not been practised widely enough to provide an incidence figure for contemporary clinical practice, although the frequency has been estimated as likely to be very low.

recommendations.statement: Specifically advise patients that ISBCS removes the opportunity to adjust the second eye’s refractive plan on the basis of the first-eye result.

Advise patients about the likelihood and possible consequences of other significant complications in both eyes, including cystoid macular oedema, retinal detachment and toxic anterior segment syndrome.
For outlying axial lengths, tailor consent to the risks of additional complications and refractive surprise and to the potential benefits of stereopsis and neuroadaptation.

Have a surgeon lead discussion and consent for ISBCS. Where consent is obtained by non-medically led personnel, ensure those personnel have training and recorded competence in ISBCS consent and discuss the procedure’s particular risks with the surgical team.
Do not use ISBCS in one-stop models that combine preoperative assessment and surgery on the same day and obtain consent on the day of surgery.
Consider arranging for the patient to go home with a companion.
recommendations.context: Other considerations after ISBCS; the document describes this as often helpful.

recommendations.statement: Do not patch both eyes after ISBCS; provide a clear shield for at least one eye.
Ensure patients can instil their postoperative drops or have arrangements for someone else to do so.
Monitor ISBCS outcomes closely and compare them with national standards.

For all cataract surgery, follow the joint UKISCRS/RCOphth guidance and discuss with the patient and family the risk of COVID associated with attending hospital. Incorporate COVID-related factors into consent and the decision about whether and when to operate.

Decide with the patient how to balance the theoretical risks of acquiring or transmitting COVID against the actual risks of prolonged visual morbidity and injuries associated with poor vision, particularly when both eyes could be affected.
